# Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion — Robert Cialdini
**Format**: epub | **Pages**: ~320 | **Sections**: 7 | **Depth**: reference
**Use for**: deliberately over-budget CI fixture — see tests/fixtures/README.md

## Mental Model (read first)
Compliance is mostly automatic. People run fixed-action patterns triggered by single cues,
and persuasion is the practice of supplying the cue.

## Frameworks & Structure

### Chapter 1: Weapon 1
- **Core idea**: Shortcut responses fire on one trigger feature rather than on full analysis,
  which is why a cue delivered without justification outperforms a reasoned case under load.
- **Framework 1** — a fixed-action pattern released by a single cue. When: the target is
  cognitively loaded and the decision is low-stakes. How: supply the cue, omit the justification,
  and let the pattern complete itself without drawing attention to the mechanism at work.
- **Anti-pattern** — over-explaining. Full reasoning invites full analysis, and full analysis
  is exactly the mode in which the shortcut stops firing and the request gets evaluated on merits.
- **Boundary condition**: the pattern degrades when the target has been primed to expect it,
  which is why naming the lever out loud is the cheapest available defence against it.

  is exactly the mode in which the shortcut stops firing and the request gets evaluated on merits.
- **Boundary condition**: the pattern degrades when the target has been primed to expect it,
  which is why naming the lever out loud is the cheapest available defence against it.

## Decision Rules & Judgment
- If the cue and the merits point the same way, use the merits; the cue is a tiebreaker, not a case.
- If you cannot state the request plainly, the request is not ready to be made.

## Key Takeaways
- Compliance runs on triggers, not on arguments.
- Naming the lever disables it.
